You use participles as adjectives: Partizip I for actions in progress (das lachende Kind, die wartenden Gäste) and Partizip II for completed actions (das gebackene Brot, die verlorenen Jahre).
The laughing child is called Ludwig.
The freshly baked bread smells wonderful.
We're making up for the lost years.
In the coming year I'm moving to Berlin.
Form Partizip I: infinitive + -d (lachen → lachend) for simultaneous, active actions.
Use Partizip II as an adjective for completed or passive actions (gebacken, verloren).
Decline participles like any adjective (der lachende Junge, ein lachendes Kind, mit lachenden Augen).
Replace a relative clause with a participle (das Kind, das lacht → das lachende Kind).
Use Partizip I as an adverb (Sie kam lachend herein).
It's 31 December 2030. The whole house is celebrating New Year's Eve at the café “Bei Ingrid”. Friedrich has come from Lübeck. Shortly before midnight, he takes Mara aside.
Mara, do you have a moment? I have to tell you something before the fireworks start.
Of course, Mr Mertens. Is everything all right? You look so serious.
Everything is more than all right. I've made a decision. In the coming year I'm moving to Berlin.
To Berlin? But your house on the Trave, your pupils…

Sophie is taking over my house. And my two pupils are good enough to carry on playing without me. I'm ninety-six, Mara. I have sixty-five lost years. I don't want to spend the few years I have left in Lübeck while Grete is in Berlin.
And where will you live? There's no lift in our house…
Two streets from here there's a care home with a garden and an old, tuned grand piano in the common room. A room there becomes free in February. And there's room for two as well.
For two? Do you mean… Mrs Hoffmann too?
If she wants. I haven't asked her yet. I wanted to ask you first, as her nurse. And as her friend. Would it be good for her?

Mr Mertens… She can't climb the stairs on her own any more. She's often alone on the fourth floor. A room with a garden, with a piano, with you… I think it would be the best thing that could happen to her.
Then I'll ask her at midnight. At the first fireworks. So that I never forget.
“eine Entscheidung treffen” = to make a decision
1. Partizip I: what someone is doing NOW
Partizip I = infinitive + -d. It shows an active, ongoing, simultaneous action (like the English “-ing” form or “who/which…”):
im kommenden Jahr (in the coming year)
As an adverb, with no ending: “Sie kam lachend herein.” = She came in laughing. “Er sitzt singend in der Badewanne.” = He sits singing in the bath.
2. Partizip II as an adjective: what has ALREADY been done
Partizip II (the participle from the Perfekt) as an adjective shows a completed or passive action (like the English past participle “baked, lost”):
das frisch gebackene Brot (the freshly baked bread)
der gestimmte Flügel (the tuned grand piano)

Comparison: “das kochende Wasser” = the boiling water (now). “das gekochte Wasser” = the boiled water (already). “ein schreibender Mann” = a man who is writing; “ein geschriebener Brief” = a written letter.
Participles used before a noun are declined exactly like adjectives (chapters 18–19):
the lost years / after the lost years
4. Participle instead of a relative clause
In writing, German often replaces a relative clause with a participle, to make it shorter:
You can also add other words between the article and the participle: “das heute Morgen frisch gebackene Brot” (the bread freshly baked this morning). You'll see this often in B2 texts.
In the coming year I'm moving.
The sleeping dog is lying under the table.
The tuned grand piano is in the common room.

That night the café “Bei Ingrid” was fuller than ever. Lit-up garlands hung in the windows, there were flickering candles in old honey jars on the tables, and from the kitchen came the smell of freshly baked doughnuts, the traditional doughnuts people eat in Berlin on New Year's Eve. Lena had baked two hundred. By eleven o'clock there were only twenty left.

In the corner, on the long bench, sat little Ludwig, two years old, with red hair and a face covered in icing sugar, between his laughing parents. He hadn't slept for two hours, even though his bedtime was long past, and he was running after every dog in the café. Fritz, who was now twelve and whiter around the muzzle than ever, patiently let his ears be pulled. Bruno was hiding under the table.
Do you remember, Mara? Exactly four years ago. New Year's Eve in A&E. Jonas burnt, the ring lost.
The ring found again. In the glove. How could I forget?

Mrs Hoffmann was sitting by the window, in her navy-blue dress, with a glass of champagne in her trembling hand. Next to her sat Friedrich, in a dark suit he had brought specially from Lübeck. They were talking quietly to each other and looked like two students in love who had hidden in a corner. Mara saw Friedrich keep looking at the old clock on the wall. He was nervous. A ninety-six-year-old man, nervous like a boy.

At a quarter to twelve, Jakob stood up and picked up his cello. Ludwig picked up his guitar. Paul, who had come from Munich with his father, picked up his. And then they played, in the packed café, among the singing customers and the playing children, old songs that everyone knew. Ludwig sang the loudest. And the most out of tune, as Mrs Hoffmann informed him, very loudly, across the whole room.

Two minutes before midnight, they all went out onto Kastanienallee, with champagne glasses in their hands and sparklers that Kuba and Ola had handed out. Mrs Hoffmann was wheeled outside in her wheelchair by Jakob and Andrei, well wrapped up in her grey blanket. Friedrich rolled along beside her. The sky over Berlin was already full of stray rockets, and the air smelt of snow and smoke.

Then the countdown began. Ten, nine, eight. The whole street was counting, from every window, from every balcony. Seven, six, five. Mara stood next to Jakob, holding his hand. Four, three, two. Friedrich took Grete's hand. One.

The sky exploded into thousands of colours. Red, green, gold, silver. People shouted, laughed, hugged each other. And in the middle of all that noise, in the light of the falling sparks, an old man in a wheelchair leaned towards an old woman in a wheelchair and said something to her that nobody heard except her.

Mara saw it from a distance. She saw Mrs Hoffmann's face, first surprised, then serious, then smiling. She saw the old pianist nod, once, slowly, and Friedrich raise her hand to his lips. She saw Ludwig, who was standing next to them, take off his glasses and wipe them for a long time. And she knew, without hearing a word, what had just happened.

Jakob had seen it too. He turned to Mara, in the flickering light of the rockets, and said: “Do you know what my resolution is for the coming year?” Mara shook her head. “No lost years,” he said. “Not one. Not even a single lost day.” Mara laughed and kissed him, in the middle of Kastanienallee, among the banging firecrackers and the dancing neighbours. Kuba, who was standing next to them, covered his eyes and shouted: “Mr Lorenz! There are children here!” Ola tugged at his sleeve. “Shush,” she said. “It's romantic.”

Later, after most of the customers had left and only the family was still sitting in the warm café, among empty glasses and burnt-down candles, Mrs Hoffmann tapped her glass with a teaspoon. Everyone fell silent.

Dear friends. I am ninety-four. I have lived through a war, a wall, a divided city and a reunited one. For sixty-five years I waited for a man who wanted to give me a bow. Tonight he asked me whether I'll move with him into a room with a garden. Two streets from here. With a tuned piano.
She paused. Nobody was breathing. Even little Ludwig, who had almost fallen asleep on Clara's lap, opened his eyes.
I said yes. We're making up for the lost years. All the ones we have left. And you, Mara, child, will still come every Wednesday. To take my blood pressure. And for tea.

The café exploded for the second time that night. Kuba jumped onto a chair and shouted: “I want to be a witness!” Ola shouted: “Me too!” Jakob laughed so hard that he dropped his cello. And Ludwig, old Ludwig, stood up, walked slowly over to Friedrich and held out his hand. “Mr Mertens,” he said, “take very good care of her. Admittedly, she holds the bow too tightly. But otherwise she's perfect.”

On New Year's morning, Kastanienallee was quiet and grey, full of rocket debris and empty bottles, and the air still smelt of smoke. At seven o'clock, Ludwig came down, as he did every morning, with Fritz, even though the bakery was closed for New Year. He went anyway. It had been his habit for fifty years. He stopped in front of the café. On the bench in front of the door sat two people in winter coats, with a flask of tea between them: Mara and Jakob, who hadn't slept. They had talked all night, about everything, about the years to come, about a child maybe, some day, about a bigger flat, perhaps in the same house. Ludwig sat down next to them without asking. Fritz lay down on his feet. “Well,” said Ludwig, “what are your resolutions?” Mara looked at Jakob. Jakob looked at Mara. “No lost years,” they both said at once. Ludwig nodded slowly. “That's the best resolution I've ever heard,” he said. “Ingrid would have made it too.” Then together they watched the first sun of the new year rise over the rooftops of Prenzlauer Berg, pale, cold and wonderful.

Behind them the bakery door opened, even though it was closed. Lena came out, with her winter coat over her pyjamas, carrying a basket full of warm rolls that she had baked at five, despite it being New Year, “out of habit”. Andrei followed her with four coffees. They all sat down together on the narrow bench, squeezed up next to one another, five people and an old dog, and had breakfast in the cold morning air, without saying much. It was, Mara thought, the most beautiful start to a year she had ever experienced.
And none of them was alone.
